name: xFreeRDP - Pass the Hash
description: Authenticates over RDP with an NT hash using /pth (Restricted Admin mode). The target must have Restricted Admin enabled: set DisableRestrictedAdmin to 0 under HKLM\System\CurrentControlSet\Control\Lsa first.

examples.label: RDP in with the NT hash

notes:
`xfreerdp /u:.. /pth:<nthash> /v:<ip>` RDPs with a hash (Restricted Admin mode must be enabled). Full GUI session without the plaintext password.
Also covered in: OSCP PEN-200 Chapter 19 (Password Attacks)

defense.why_it_works: NTLM/Kerberos authenticate the account's SECRET (its NT hash or Kerberos key), not the plaintext password — the KDC/target never sees the password itself. So possessing the hash/ticket is equivalent to knowing the password: you inject it and authenticate as that user without ever cracking it. With Restricted Admin mode, FreeRDP can authenticate to RDP using only the NT hash.
defense.prerequisites: A valid NTLM hash, RDP reachable, and Restricted Admin mode enabled on the target.
defense.impact: An RDP session as the target account via PtH.
defense.detection: [MITRE T1550.002] Event 4624 Logon Type 3 with Authentication Package NTLM and LogonProcessName NtLmSsp, with NO preceding interactive logon for that account; the same NTLM hash authenticating from an unusual source; 4672 for privileged PtH.
defense.artifacts: An NTLM network logon (4624 type 3) from xfreerdp /pth; a session as the target user without their plaintext password.
defense.prevention: Enable Credential Guard and disable NTLM where possible; [MITRE T1550.002 M1026 Privileged Account Management] never reuse local-admin passwords (LAPS) so one hash doesn't unlock the network; restrict lateral admin logons; monitor NTLM auth.
defense.evasion: PtH uses valid material so no password failures occur - it blends with normal NTLM auth; using an allowed source host and common hours reduces suspicion.
defense.misconfiguration: NTLM authentication is enabled on the network and the same local administrator password (or domain credential NTLM hash) is valid across multiple machines. When LSASS holds an NTLM hash in memory (from an interactive logon), any process running as SYSTEM can extract it and authenticate to remote services without knowing the plaintext password.
defense.vulnerable_config:
# Machines with identical local admin passwords (the classic PtH enabler)
# No credential guard, no Protected Users group
# NTLM enabled (default on all Windows versions)

# Confirm NTLM is negotiated (SMB example):
# Network capture shows NTLMSSP_AUTH frames on port 445

# Accounts NOT in Protected Users group (PtH works against these):
Get-ADGroupMember 'Protected Users'  # should list all privileged accounts

# Local admin SID S-1-5-21-...-500 (RID 500) allows remote PtH by default
# Even with UAC RemoteRestrictions, RID-500 bypasses the filter
defense.secure_config:
# 1. Enable Credential Guard (blocks NTLM hash extraction from LSASS)
# GPO: Computer Configuration > Admin Templates > System > Device Guard
#   'Turn on Virtualization Based Security' = Enabled
#   'Credential Guard Configuration' = Enabled with UEFI lock

# 2. Add privileged accounts to Protected Users group (no NTLM, no RC4)
Add-ADGroupMember -Identity 'Protected Users' -Members 'Domain Admins'

# 3. LAPS — unique random local admin passwords per machine
# Eliminates lateral movement via shared local admin hash
Enable-LapsADSchema
Set-LAPSConfig -PolicyMode Automatic -PasswordLength 20 -PasswordAgeDays 30

# 4. Block NTLM (requires AES Kerberos everywhere first)
# GPO: Security Settings > Local Policies > Security Options
#   'Network Security: Restrict NTLM: Incoming NTLM traffic' = Deny all

# 5. Disable RID-500 remote admin:
# HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Policies\System
#   LocalAccountTokenFilterPolicy = 0 (default)
